prompt.context: Our client is The Dalt Wisney Company, a diversified entertainment company known for its iconic franchises and unparalleled storytelling for the whole family. Colloquially known as the 'Home of Gnome' for its first beloved character, Nellie Gnome, Wisney recently launched its own direct-to-consumer SVOD (streaming video on demand) service, Wisney+, filled with the rich content library of Wisney's film and TV studios. However, this week, Wisney's competitor WanderMedia announced that it will be releasing its entire slate of movies simultaneously in theaters and on its own streaming platform, WanderMax, rather than the typical windowing in which films play exclusively in theaters for 90 days.
prompt.question: The CEO of Wisney wants to know: why did WanderMedia make the switch, and more importantly, should Wisney follow?

clarifying_info.q: What business segments does Wisney operate in?
clarifying_info.a: Operations include content production (traditional movie/TV studios), media distribution (owned SVOD platform Wisney+ and content licensing), consumer products (toys, apparel, books), and theme parks.

clarifying_info.q: How does Wisney generate revenue from its content?
clarifying_info.a: Three main channels: (1) Theatrical — consumers buy tickets from movie theaters who split box office revenues with movie studios; (2) Streaming — consumers purchase subscriptions to Wisney+, which offers its entire library on demand for a single monthly fee (no pay-per-view); (3) Licensing — fees paid by networks (e.g. CBS) or other streaming platforms (e.g. Netflix) for the right to show content.
Wisney wants to maximize profits while maintaining its long-term position as the leading family entertainment company in the United States.

exhibits.title: Number of movie tickets sold and average ticket price in the U.S. and Canada; SVOD subscription households; Monthly costs of SVOD platforms in the U.S. in 2019
exhibits.shows: Three charts: (1) a dual-axis time-series (1980–2025E) showing number of movie tickets sold in millions (left axis) and average ticket price in U.S. dollars (right axis); (2) a bar chart of SVOD subscription households showing 125 million in 2019 and 350 million estimated in 2025; (3) a bar chart of monthly costs of SVOD platforms in 2019 (Netflix $9.99, Amazon $9.99, Dalt Wisney $6.99, Hulu $7.99, WanderMedia $14.99)
exhibits.data: 2025E tickets sold: 1,200 million; 2025E avg ticket price: ~$10; SVOD subscribers 2025E: 350 million; Wisney+ monthly price: $6.99; WanderMedia monthly price: $14.99; Netflix/Amazon: $9.99; Hulu: $7.99

framework: Why did WanderMedia switch? — Internal factors: financial (box office revenues: ticket volume, price, theater split; subscription fees: subscribers, price, churn; licensing fees; production/marketing costs) and operational (content library depth, talent relationships, distribution infrastructure)

Why did WanderMedia switch? — External factors: audience (market size of theatrical vs. streaming, preferences, willingness to pay); competing studios and SVOD platforms; major movie theater chains and their leverage
Should Wisney follow? — Assess whether Wisney faces similar financial implications (revenue mix from theatrical vs. streaming)
Should Wisney follow? — Assess whether Wisney faces similar operational implications (content pipeline, talent, platform maturity)
Should Wisney follow? — Assess whether Wisney faces similar external implications (audience overlap, theater relationships, competitive landscape)

questions.prompt: Which segment will be larger in 2025 — theatrical movies or streaming subscriptions? Size each market.
questions.guidance: Candidate should request data to size each market (ticket volumes, prices, revenue splits, subscriber counts, subscription prices). After receiving Exhibit 1 they should discuss trends (streaming growing rapidly, theatrical recovering post-COVID but still smaller) and then calculate 2025 market sizes. A strong candidate notes that households can hold multiple SVOD subscriptions, making the streaming estimate conservative.

math.setup: Theatrical market size = tickets sold × avg ticket price × studio's share of box office. Streaming market size = SVOD subscribers × monthly subscription price × 12 months.
math.answer: Streaming market ($42B) will be $36 billion larger than the theatrical market ($6B) in 2025.

questions.prompt: Calculate the average customer lifetime value (CLV) of a theatrical moviegoer vs. a streaming subscriber. Assume: individuals are exclusively one type, discount rate = 0%, both have a 90% retention rate. Avg ticket = $10, customers see 4 movies/year, 50/50 theater split. Avg subscription = $10/month, 4 people share one account.
questions.guidance: Candidate should recall the CLV formula. With 0% discount rate, CLV simplifies to ARPU / churn rate (churn = 1 − retention = 10%). Candidate should set up annual revenue per customer for each segment, then apply the multiplier. A strong candidate notes that different acquisition costs would affect net CLV, and that in reality moviegoing and streaming can be complementary rather than mutually exclusive.

math.setup: CLV = ARPU × (1 + r) / (1 + r − retention) = ARPU / churn when discount rate = 0%. Churn = 1 − 0.90 = 0.10. Multiplier = 1 / 0.10 = 10.
steps: Difference: $300 − $200 = $100 higher CLV for streaming customers
math.answer: Theatrical CLV = $200; Streaming CLV = $300. Streaming customers are worth $100 more over their lifetime.

questions.prompt: What are additional ways Wisney could increase profits from its SVOD platform, Wisney+?
questions.guidance: Candidate should impose a clear 2×2 or similar structure (e.g. existing vs. new customers × increase revenues vs. decrease costs). Ideas should be specific and actionable. Push for creativity beyond the obvious price increase.

questions.prompt: Calculate the expected change in lifetime value if Wisney switches to simultaneous release. Assumptions: 50% of moviegoers would become exclusive SVOD subscribers; likelihood of movie theater retaliation (no longer showing Wisney films) = 75%; Wisney expects to sell 320 million movie tickets in the coming year.
questions.guidance: Candidate must set up a probability-weighted expected value comparing current LV of the moviegoing segment to the expected LV after the switch under two scenarios (retaliation / no retaliation). Should conclude that the expected loss makes simultaneous release not worthwhile.

math.setup: Current moviegoers = 320M tickets / 4 tickets per person per year = 80M customers. Current LV = 80M × $200 = $16B. After switch: 50% become SVOD subscribers, 50% remain theatrical. Two scenarios: (A) no retaliation (p=25%) and (B) retaliation — theaters drop Wisney (p=75%).
steps: No Retaliation (25%): Theater segment = 80M × $200 × 50% = $8B; SVOD segment = 80M × $300 × 50% = $12B; Total = $20B
math.answer: Expected loss of $2 billion in lifetime value. Not worth the risk.

brainstorming.prompt: What are additional ways Wisney could increase profits from its SVOD platform, Wisney+?

categories.name: Increase Revenue from Existing Customers
ideas: Introduce pay-per-view pricing for new film releases
Introduce tiered subscription levels (ad-supported vs. ad-free)
Limit or charge for sharing of subscription accounts
Increase personalization to reduce churn and retain subscribers longer

categories.name: Increase Revenue from New Customers
ideas: Create exclusive platform content targeting new markets (e.g. foreign-language originals, niche fan bases)
Bundle Wisney+ with other SVOD or telecom services to attract new subscribers

categories.name: Decrease Costs for Existing Customers
ideas: Use in-platform promotions of new content to reduce external marketing spend
Benchmark efficiency of in-house content production to identify cost savings

categories.name: Decrease Costs for New Customers
ideas: Evaluate customer acquisition costs across channels and benchmark against competition
Achieve greater economies of scale as subscriber base grows

recommendation: No — Wisney should not follow WanderMedia's strategy of simultaneous theatrical and streaming release.

Although streaming CLV ($300) exceeds theatrical CLV ($200), the 75% probability that major theater chains retaliate (as Cinedot did with WanderMedia) creates an expected lifetime value loss of $2 billion, making the switch financially destructive.
risks: By maintaining the traditional release window, Wisney potentially risks ceding streaming market share to competitors who do pursue simultaneous release strategies.
If WanderMedia's simultaneous release attracts subscribers and proves successful, Wisney may face pressure to follow regardless.
next_steps: Find other ways to differentiate Wisney+ and grow its subscription base without antagonizing theater chains — e.g. exclusive original content, bundling with other products or services.
Monitor WanderMedia's results and theater chain reactions closely to reassess the risk calculus over time.
